one_line_reason: A clinical practice guideline and multiple systematic reviews/RCTs address oral feverfew for migraine prevention, with an overall mixed-to-modestly-positive picture worth central verification.

selected.population: adults with episodic migraine (evidence base of 49 Class I/II migraine-prevention studies)
selected.dose_as_stated: not stated in this guideline abstract
selected.why_selected: AAN/AHS evidence-based practice guideline rates feverfew (MIG-99) 'probably effective' (Level B) for migraine prevention, the highest-authority source in the shortlist.

selected.population: adults with migraine (Cochrane systematic review, 5 RCTs, 343 patients)
selected.intervention: oral feverfew extract vs placebo for migraine prevention
selected.why_selected: the definitive Cochrane systematic review; concludes evidence is mixed and insufficient to convincingly establish efficacy over placebo, an important counterweight to the guideline.

selected.population: women with chronic migraine (n=69, randomized to acupuncture, feverfew (TAN), or both)
selected.intervention: Tanacetum parthenium (feverfew) monotherapy arm, oral, daily
selected.primary_outcome: quality of life (SF-36), migraine disability (MIDAS), pain (VAS)
selected.why_selected: one of the few shortlisted trials with a standalone oral feverfew-only arm and a stated daily dose, showing improvement (though less than the combined acupuncture+feverfew arm).

selected.population: migraineurs with mild-headache-phase attacks (n=60, treating 208 evaluable attacks)
selected.intervention: sublingual feverfew/ginger (LipiGesic M) taken at earliest recognition of migraine, vs placebo
selected.dose_as_stated: not stated (sublingual preparation, dose per administration not given)
selected.primary_outcome: pain-free and pain-relief rates at 2 hours for acute migraine
selected.why_selected: positive double-blind RCT for acute (not just preventive) use, though it combines feverfew with ginger in a sublingual, not standard oral, form.

blockers: Feverfew is most often studied and dosed as standardized extract by parthenolide content, but the individual trial doses are not given in these abstracts, so mapping to catalog label amounts (mg feverfew leaf vs. mg parthenolide) is uncertain.
The largest, most rigorous trial identified across the Cochrane reviews found no significant difference from placebo, so the overall evidence for prevention is genuinely mixed, not clearly positive.
Two of the four selected trials combine feverfew with another ingredient (ginger, or acupuncture) or use a non-oral-capsule route (sublingual), complicating isolation of feverfew's own effect.

excluded_pmids.reason: Broad systematic review of 9 different herbal treatments for migraine (feverfew, butterbur, curcumin, etc.); reports feverfew findings as 'mixed' without a feverfew-specific effect size, and positive conclusions in the review are mainly about butterbur.
Earlier (2000) Cochrane review of feverfew for migraine prevention, superseded by the more complete 2004 Cochrane review (PMID 14973986) already selected.
2000 narrative update of the same trial base covered by the Cochrane reviews; no new primary data beyond what is captured by the selected Cochrane review.
1998 systematic review of the same early feverfew migraine trials, superseded by later Cochrane reviews already represented in the selection.
Narrative review restating findings from the same trial base as the Cochrane reviews; no new primary data.
General pharmacist-education article surveying many herbs' safety profiles; not a primary study or focused review of feverfew efficacy.
Open-label (not blinded), uncontrolled-arm study of a feverfew+willow bark combination product (Mig-RL); weak design and combination formulation, not single-ingredient feverfew evidence.

Primarily in vitro and animal anti-inflammatory mechanism study of a parthenolide-depleted feverfew extract; the only human data point is a topical methyl-nicotinate skin vasodilation/erythema model, not an oral supplement efficacy outcome.
